idiom_name: class handle with deinit (ARC) + defer for scope-bound hand-back
implementation_notes: Swift's release point is deinit, called immediately before a class instance is deallocated - the language's own deinitializer example returns the resource to its owner at that moment. For borrowed resources the scope-bound form is defer { owner.release(r) } right after the checkout, and a small class handle whose deinit hands back is the wrapper form that survives being stored. Express ownership in the type you return: a class handle (deterministic deinit when the last reference goes away) rather than a struct, because value semantics copy the handle and would hand the same resource back twice. The classic C++ structure maps onto a reference-typed handle and stays justified whenever the resource outlives one scope.
pitfalls: ARC release is deterministic only for the last reference: a handle stored in a long-lived cache, closure or reference cycle delays or prevents deinit, and the pool never sees the return.
Value types copy: a struct wrapper carrying the handle is duplicated on assignment, so two 'owners' hand the same resource back twice - use a class for the guard.

The optimizer may keep references alive longer than the lexical scope suggests, so when the hand-back must be observable at a specific point use defer or withExtendedLifetime rather than relying on deinit timing alone.
